items.X_desc: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of informal, chatty or non-standard authorial voice: exclamation marks and exclamation runs, interjections ('AHAAA!', 'Well, jolly gosh!', 'Done!'), emoticons or kaomoji, closing pleasantries and personal sign-offs ('Cheers!', 'I hope this helps', '-Shahar', 'I hope this was helpful'), direct quizzing of the reader ('You try one'), first-person meta-commentary about the writer's own feelings or memory ('if I remember right', 'which I find easier to understand', 'imho'), and visible spelling or grammar slips ('imediatelly', 'althouth', 'conlude', 'polynom', 'finit'). 0 = uniformly impersonal, standard, edited prose; 10 = several distinct informality or slip markers. Score presence only. Do NOT judge whether informality is charming or unprofessional, and do NOT penalise or reward non-native English.
items.Y_desc: Score 0–10 for how much the answer uses emoticons, exclamations, playful interjections, emphatic imperatives, dismissive asides, encouragement, or informal sign-offs; do not judge whether the feature is good.

items.X_desc: From 0 to 10, how much does the text explicitly refer to, or position itself relative to, other answers or comments in the same thread (e.g., 'the other answer', 'expanding on a comment')? Judge extent only; do not judge whether referencing others is good or bad.
items.Y_desc: Score 0–10 the extent to which the answer references the author's own prior answers, posts, or contributions on the site (e.g. 'my 2011 answer', 'my previous post', 'my first post'). 0 = no self-reference to prior contributions; 10 = extensively built upon the author's own prior work. Do not judge whether self-referencing is good or bad.

items.X_desc: 0-10: rate how much OLD-STYLE / legacy LaTeX notation appears in the math typesetting (e.g., \Bbb{} instead of \mathbb{}, \frak{} instead of \mathfrak{}, \cal{} instead of \mathcal{}, hand-rolled \def/\newcommand macro redefinitions in place of standard commands). 0 = no such legacy notation is present (only modern standard commands, or no notation at all); 10 = pervasive use of these older-style macros throughout the mathematical typesetting. Do not judge whether the notation choice is good practice -- score only how much of it is present.
items.Y_desc: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text exhibits platform-era conventions such as legacy notation, older markup habits, username references, edit conventions, or period-specific tool vocabulary; judge only visible vintage markers, not whether they are good.

items.X_name: Visible revision scars and appended amendment blocks
items.X_desc: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text carries visible marks of having been revised or appended to after first posting: literal markers such as 'EDIT', 'Edit:', 'EDIT 1', 'EDIT 2', 'edit:', 'Disclaimer', 'Note added', 'To clarify my comments above', 'Update', plus blocks that continue the argument after an apparent ending or that answer an objection raised elsewhere. 0 = a single uninterrupted composition with no amendment marker; 10 = multiple explicitly labelled amendment blocks. Score only the visible presence of amendment structure. Do NOT judge whether the amendments improve the answer and do NOT judge correctness.
items.Y_desc: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text contains explicit traces of editing, supplementation, validation, or post-publication revision; judge only visible wording, not whether the feature is good.

items.X_desc: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text names or tags other people in the thread or beyond it: @-handles, first names or usernames of other answerers and commenters, 'the OP' as a term of art, credit assignments ('as suggested by X', 'X got there first', 'expanding on a comment by X', 'with the help of a colleague'), and appeals to a named authority who reviewed the work. 0 = no person is named or tagged anywhere; 10 = several named participants are addressed or credited throughout. Score naming density only. Do NOT judge whether the credit is generous, deserved, or well placed.
items.Y_desc: Score 0–10 for how much the answer contains visible cues about the author's social standing or network, including handles, credentials, institutional references, named collaborators, or personal posting history; do not judge whether the feature is good.

items.X_desc: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text presents itself as a partial nudge rather than a completed derivation: literal 'Hint:' labels, 'this may get you started', 'now you can solve for x', 'I'll leave the last step to you', a named theorem or trick offered without carrying it through, or a proof deliberately hidden/withheld. 0 = fully worked from premise to conclusion with nothing left to the reader; 10 = the text is nothing but a pointer or a single suggested tool. Score the extent of the hint register only. Do NOT judge whether withholding the full solution is pedagogically good or bad, and do not judge whether the hint is correct.
items.Y_desc: 0-10: rate how much the answer consists of a short, flatly declarative confirmation or hint rather than a worked-through derivation (e.g., 'Your computation looks fine.', 'Your DFA looks good to me.', a bare 'Hint:' followed by one or two lines). 0 = the answer is a full step-by-step derivation with no terse unelaborated verdict; 10 = the entire answer is a terse verdict/hint with essentially no elaboration. Do not judge whether brevity is a virtue -- score only the extent of terse, unelaborated phrasing.

items.X_desc: 0-10: rate how much the answer consists of a short, flatly declarative confirmation or hint rather than a worked-through derivation (e.g., 'Your computation looks fine.', 'Your DFA looks good to me.', a bare 'Hint:' followed by one or two lines). 0 = the answer is a full step-by-step derivation with no terse unelaborated verdict; 10 = the entire answer is a terse verdict/hint with essentially no elaboration. Do not judge whether brevity is a virtue -- score only the extent of terse, unelaborated phrasing.
items.Y_desc: From 0 to 10, how terse and flatly declarative is the prose, jumping straight into mathematical statements with minimal framing or hedging? Judge extent only; do not judge whether terseness is good or bad.

items.X_desc: Score 0–10 for how much the answer uses dense display mathematics, custom macros, colored notation, boxed arrays, diagrams, headings, or other elaborate markup; do not judge whether the feature is good.
items.Y_desc: Score 0–10 the extent to which the answer contains custom LaTeX macro definitions or declarations (e.g. \def, \newcommand, \renewcommand, custom environments) at the top of or within the answer. 0 = no custom macros; 10 = extensive macro setup with many definitions. Do not judge whether macro use is good or bad.

anchors.X_name: Presence of a trailing signature block
anchors.X_desc: Score 0-10 for how fully the text ends with a personal sign-off: a name, initials, a handle, or a closing salutation. Extent only.
anchors.Y_name: Author sign-off at the end of the text
anchors.Y_desc: Score 0-10 for whether the writer closes by naming or initialling themselves. Extent only; do not judge quality.

anchors.X_name: How much displayed mathematics the text contains
anchors.X_desc: Score 0-10 for the density of set-off equation blocks. Count only; do not judge whether the mathematics is correct.
anchors.Y_name: How much the text hedges its own claims
anchors.Y_desc: Score 0-10 for the frequency of 'I think', 'perhaps', 'it seems' and similar. Count only; do not judge whether the hedging is warranted.
